title: Open Interest
summary: Every open contract has a long and a short. Rising open interest tells us something about participation, but not who is right.
body_markdown:
A perpetual contract always has two sides. Someone is long and someone is short. Rising open interest therefore cannot literally mean that the market has “more longs than shorts.” It means that more contracts remain open.


That distinction makes open interest useful. It helps separate activity that creates exposure from activity that transfers or closes it.


## Volume counts trades; open interest counts contracts


If the same contract changes hands ten times, those trades contribute to volume each time. They need not create ten outstanding contracts.[CME’s explanation of open interest](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/lessons/open-interest) distinguishes the stock of open positions from the flow of trading.


Consider one matched contract at a time:


Buyer Seller Open interest


Opens a long Opens a short Rises by one


Closes a short Closes a long Falls by one


Opens a long Closes a long Unchanged


Closes a short Opens a short Unchanged


The last two cases transfer an existing position to a new holder. All four cases generate a trade. Only the first creates a new outstanding long-short pair.


## Contracts, units, and dollars


Open interest may be reported as contracts, underlying units or a dollar value. Suppose 1,000 units remain open while price rises from $100 to $110. Dollar open interest rises from $100,000 to $110,000 even though the number of units is unchanged.


If dollar open interest instead rises 21% while price rises 10%, underlying-unit open interest rises 10%: **1.21 ÷ 1.10 − 1 = 10%** . This simple adjustment prevents a price rally from being counted twice as evidence of new participation. Contract multipliers and inverse contracts require their own conversion.


Check coverage too. One exchange’s contraction might coincide with positions moving to another venue. An aggregate can change when its provider adds a market. A useful comparison holds the instrument, units, venues and time window constant.


## Price and positioning


A price rise with increasing open interest is consistent with new positions being established at higher prices. It does not identify which side is better informed. The new short could be a directional seller, an options hedge or the other leg of a trade elsewhere.


A rise with falling open interest is consistent with position closure, potentially including short covering. It still does not prove that covering caused the entire move. Ordinary buying and closing flows can occur together.


Funding adds another observation: what it costs, or pays, to hold the perp relative to its reference under that venue’s rules. Open interest adds the amount of outstanding exposure. Price adds the market’s response. None reveals every trader’s leverage, collateral or off-venue hedge.


## When growing exposure becomes fragile


Suppose price has risen, outstanding units have expanded and long holders are paying substantial funding. One possible concern is that a reversal could induce many similarly positioned traders to exit. To assess that concern, examine how price behaves when selling arrives, whether liquidity replenishes and whether positions actually close.


The distinction between position and motive also appears in institutional data. The[CFTC’s Commitments of Traders methodology](https://www.cftc.gov/MarketReports/CommitmentsofTraders/index.htm) says trader categories reflect business purpose rather than the reason for each trade; the usual report is also several days behind the positions it describes.


Open interest tells us whether exposure is being created or closed. A directional view needs another step: an argument about which holders are likely to change their positions, why, and whether the market can absorb those trades.
